1.pericope_label: Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand
debates: When the feast fell
Why the vessels were sent for
Where the chapter belongs
outliers: Clarke holds that this chapter stands out of its place and should come in after the seventh and eighth

Keil and Delitzsch reject an interpreter who supposed the vessels were fetched to court the favour of the God of the Jews during the siege, since that does not harmonise with the celebration of so riotous a festival
themes: A feast proclaimed where a fast was called for
Holy vessels fetched to carry ordinary wine
A besieging army counting on the wine
A house whose posts are pulled out by its owner

3.pericope_label: Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them
debates: Whether only the golden vessels were brought
What the praising of the gods amounted to
What part the wine played
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch go beyond an interpreter who said the act placed the God of Israel on a perfect level with the heathen gods, holding that it raised those gods above him, as Daniel afterwards charges the king
Calvin refuses to lay the praise of the false gods at the door of drunkenness, and makes the wine only a stimulus to an impiety already seated in the heart
themes: Vessels carried from one temple into another
A song of thanks sung over stolen cups
Gods named by the stuff they are made of
An impiety that needed only a stimulus

5.pericope_label: In the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king’s palace
debates: Whose hand it was
Who saw what
Whether the terror did any good
outliers: Ellicott observes that only a portion of the hand was seen by the king, that we are not told whether the guests saw it, and that in other scriptural manifestations a part has been witnessed by many while the whole was seen by one or a few
Calvin makes the previously bare wall part of the evidence, since a hand standing there from the first might have been suspected of artifice
themes: Fingers gathered about a pen
A wall that was bare a moment before
A banquet that outlasted the daylight
Knees that would not hold a king up

7.pericope_label: The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. And the king spake, and said to the wise men of Babylon, Whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet
debates: Why Daniel was not called at first
Why the wise men could not read it
What the third place was
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch call altogether untenable the supposition that the king summoned only three classes on purpose to avoid Daniel, out of a heathen religious fear of the God of the Jews
Ellicott sets aside three conjectures about the script, the language and the arrangement of the words, and rests the whole difficulty on the supernatural character of the inscription
themes: A king shouting at his own table
A counsellor daily in sight and never called
Letters that would not be read
A report that travelled as far as the conqueror

10.pericope_label: Now the queen, by reason of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banquet house: and the queen spake and said, O king, live for ever: let not thy thoughts trouble thee
debates: Who the queen was
Whether father means ancestor or predecessor
What the excellent spirit was
outliers: Calvin refuses to decide between the wife and the grandmother and says it is better to suspend judgment than to assert anything rashly, where Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch all argue for one identification or another

Gill distinguishes the excellent spirit the queen praised, which he takes for natural knowledge and political wisdom, from a further excellent spirit of real grace and piety which he says she knew nothing of
themes: An old woman walking into a drunken hall
A counsellor recommended last who should have been first
A name given by a king long dead
Knots that one man could untie

13.pericope_label: Then was Daniel brought in before the king. And the king spake and said unto Daniel, Art thou that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Jewry?
debates: How the king addressed him
What the spirit of the gods meant on his lips
What the renewed offer of reward showed
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch notice that the king drops the word holy which the queen had used with the very same phrase about the spirit of the gods
Calvin reads the offer of the third place as evidence that the terror had already worn off, since the king promises wealth and honours as though his kingdom would stand, on the last night of it
themes: A man fetched from a house nobody had visited
A king who knew his prophet only by hearsay
Knots that a judge is called on to untie
Honours offered on the last night of a reign

17.pericope_label: Then Daniel answered and said before the king, Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another; yet I will read the writing unto the king
debates: Why Daniel refused the gifts here and not before
Why the speech begins a generation back
What the majesty was for
outliers: Calvin explains the refusal by the difference between the two kings, since some feelings of honour remained in the grandfather while the grandson was at his last extremity, and adds that an outright refusal of the purple at the end would have looked like timidity or treason
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the long description of the power of Nebuchadnezzar has the undeniable object of impressing on Belshazzar that he did not equal his father
themes: Rewards refused from a king with hours to live
A speech that begins a generation back
Thousands consenting to be ruled by one
A balance in which a man is found wanting

20.pericope_label: But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him
debates: Who put the heart among the beasts
Why the old story is retold
What the profanation added to the pride
outliers: Calvin canvasses whether the verb makes the king assimilate his own senses to the brutes or makes God infatuate him so as to render him like them, and leaves both readings standing
Ellicott holds the king overran the limits of an authority he really had, since the Israelites were his subjects by right of conquest but their God was not his to blaspheme
themes: A palace exchanged for a field of wild asses
An example that should have lasted a thousand years
Sacred cups passed among concubines
A breath held in another hand

24.pericope_label: Then was the part of the hand sent from him; and this writing was written. And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN
debates: Why the Chaldeans could not read it
Why the first word is doubled
What the last word carries
outliers: Clarke explains the failure by the script, holding that the words stood in the old Hebrew character which the Jews used before the captivity and which the Chaldeans did not know, where Calvin holds they were simply struck blind, since they could have read it otherwise
Ellicott reports a conjecture that the second occurrence of the first word was originally the name of Media, which he calls plausible but without external support
themes: A hand sent, and no spectre
Letters legible to one man in the room
A number that cannot be added to
Tyrants whose years are already counted

26.pericope_label: This is the interpretation of the thing: MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting
debates: Why the first word is doubled
Why two nations are named
Why the king kept his promise
outliers: Calvin holds there was properly no division of the kingdom at all, the city being taken by one conqueror who then admitted his father-in-law to share the royal authority, so that the two names stand for a doubled disgrace rather than a partition
Calvin rejects the view that the king kept his promise because the word of a Babylonian king was held binding, and reads the whole ceremony as a display of unconcern put on for the nobles
themes: A balance God keeps and does not lend
A kingdom broken off and handed over
Purple put on a man who had refused it
A king performing calm for his own court

30.pericope_label: In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old
debates: Who killed the king
Who Darius the Median was
What the beginning of the fulfilment proved
outliers: Calvin rejects the story that a guard stabbed the king on hearing the voice of the prophet, since the sentence of God does not depend on the will of a single heathen

Ellicott admits that Darius the Median cannot be identified with any person in profane history and that no trace of the name has been found in the inscriptions of the period, and rests the case on the accuracy of the book elsewhere
themes: A river turned out of its bed
Doors opened by the king to ask what the noise was
A man in purple standing untouched in a sacked palace
A head of gold giving way to arms of silver
